title: NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet Multiplane Network Architecture at Hot Chips 2026
gist: At Hot Chips 2026 NVIDIA pitched its Spectrum-X Ethernet multiplane topology as the way to scale a single AI factory's scale-out fabric 64x, from 8k to 512k Rubin GPUs at 1.6T per GPU, while claiming 1.7x fewer switches and fault recovery that holds 90% bandwidth where traditional topologies drop to zero. The through-line is that AI factories need five purpose-built, co-designed networks rather than general-purpose Ethernet, a framing that lands as a direct shot at Broadcom's same-day Thor Ultra presentation.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's Spectrum-X multiplane topology splits each GPU's 1.6Tbps scale-out link into 8x 200Gbps connections to different switches, letting planes share switch hardware instead of dedicating full rails.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is the core architectural mechanism behind NVIDIA's next scaling step for AI networking; it reshapes switch, NIC, and optics demand per GPU.
insights.quote: Instead of 1.6Tbps to one switch, this is 8x 200Gbps, with each link going to a different switch.
insights.locator: Now NVIDIA introduces the multiplane topology

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims multiplane extends AI-factory scale-out 64x over multi-rail, reaching 512k Rubin GPUs at 1.6T per-GPU bandwidth using 100T switches with 512 ports of 200G laid out as eight planes across four rails.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Half-million-GPU single fabrics are the design target for next-gen AI factories, implying enormous per-cluster networking and optics content for NVIDIA.
insights.quote: Multiplane extends AI factory scale by 64x over multi-rail. NVIDIA lands at 512k Rubin GPUs, still at 1.6T scale-out bandwidth per GPU
insights.locator: Multiplane extends AI factory scale by 64x

insights.claim: The multi-rail baseline NVIDIA is moving beyond tops out at 8k Rubin GPUs at 1.6T per-GPU scale-out bandwidth, with 100T switches carrying 64 ports of 1.6T split across four rails.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Sets the 8k-to-512k scaling delta that justifies the multiplane architecture; the topology change, not faster ports, is what buys scale.
insights.locator: Multi-rail is the first step up

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims the multiplane topology needs 1.7x fewer scale-out switches than a traditional multi-tier single-rail topology, cutting power, rack space, and cost.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Fewer switches per GPU compresses the addressable switch TAM per cluster even as cluster sizes explode; watch how merchant-switch vendors respond.
insights.locator: Multiplane also trims the physical footprint

themes.theme: Fault tolerance as the selling point

insights.claim: Under partial bandwidth loss, NVIDIA's Spectrum-X multiplane topology holds 90% bandwidth with 2.68ms fault detection, while a traditional multi-tier topology drops to 0% bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: At 512k-GPU scale, failures are constant; graceful degradation versus total loss is the economic argument for buying the whole NVIDIA fabric stack.
insights.quote: the Spectrum-X multiplane topology holds 90% bandwidth with a 2.68ms detection time, while a traditional multi-tier topology drops to 0% bandwidth
insights.locator: Fault behavior is where multiplane is meant

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims Spectrum-X detects faults roughly 400x faster (2.68ms) and recovers about 11x faster (100ms) than off-the-shelf Ethernet multiplane, which suffers full bandwidth loss with 1080ms detection and recovery, converting to a 1.6x goodput advantage.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The goodput framing turns a networking spec into a GPU-utilization ROI argument, the metric hyperscaler buyers actually price.

themes.theme: Purpose-built networks thesis and the Broadcom subtext

insights.claim: NVIDIA divides the AI factory into five purpose-built networks (scale-across, scale-in, scale-out, scale-up, and AI context scale) and argues a single general-purpose fabric cannot serve all of them well, which is the load-bearing claim of the entire talk.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: If the five-network framing wins, buyers get pulled into full-stack NVIDIA fabrics rather than mixing merchant silicon; it is the strategic moat argument.
insights.quote: A single general-purpose fabric cannot serve all of these well, and that is the load-bearing claim behind the rest of the talk.
insights.locator: Here NVIDIA divides the AI factory

insights.claim: NVIDIA is positioning directly against Broadcom: 'scale-in' was unveiled right after Broadcom's Thor Ultra presentation at Hot Chips 2026, and NVIDIA quipped that '100G SerDes is last year's stuff' immediately after Broadcom presented a 100G SerDes part.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Signals an escalating NVIDIA-vs-Broadcom fight for AI Ethernet; NVIDIA is leaning on 200G SerDes and co-packaged optics as its generational edge.
insights.quote: “100G SerDes is last year’s stuff” just after Broadcom presents 100G SerDes Thor Ultra at Hot Chips. Awesome.
insights.locator: Spectrum-X Ethernet photonics is the production

insights.claim: NVIDIA's closing argument is that Ethernet can handle AI-factory scale-out only when the hardware is purpose-designed for AI, and the author cautions the real test is whether the claimed figures hold in live deployments.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Vendor-slide multipliers are unproven at deployment scale; watch early 512k-class buildouts for validation before extrapolating share shifts.
insights.quote: Whether those figures hold in live deployments is the real test

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims Spectrum-X delivers 1.6x higher RDMA bandwidth, 2.2x better multi-tenancy, and 1.3x lower bandwidth jitter versus alternatives, built around 102.4T switch systems and 1.6T SuperNICs, with jitter solved end-to-end rather than per device.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The end-to-end system framing is the lock-in: the claimed gains require NVIDIA NICs plus NVIDIA switches together.

insights.claim: In a multi-tenant DeepSeek V3 multi-job training run, NVIDIA claims Spectrum-X delivers 1.9x higher training performance than off-the-shelf Ethernet, with the step-time gap widening over 80-plus steps due to low-jitter communications and tenant noise isolation.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Multi-tenant noise isolation is the neocloud/hyperscaler pain point; a 1.9x training delta is a large TCO wedge against generic Ethernet.

insights.claim: For key NCCL operations in Nemotron Ultra pre-training, NVIDIA claims gradient all-reduce runs 14x faster on Spectrum-X than off-the-shelf Ethernet, token dispatch 3.5x, and gradient reduce-scatter and parallel matrix multiply 2x each.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Shows how hardware-software co-design (NCCL tuned to the fabric) produces gains merchant silicon cannot match without NVIDIA's software stack.
insights.locator: Extreme co-design is most evident in NCCL

insights.claim: NVIDIA puts optics at 10% of the compute power in an AI factory, well above what a conventional cloud data center carries, making optics a first-order cost and power line in AI buildouts.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Rising optical intensity per AI dollar is the demand driver for the optics supply chain (lasers, photonics, transceivers); 10% of compute power is a big anchor number.
insights.quote: NVIDIA puts the optical share in an AI factory at 10% of the compute power, well above what a conventional cloud data center typically carries.

insights.claim: NVIDIA has a co-packaged optics chip with micro ring modulators in production and a 3D-stacked silicon photonics engine on TSMC's Coupe process, claiming 4x fewer lasers, lower power, and 10x lower mean time between interruptions.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: CPO in production shifts value from pluggable transceiver makers toward NVIDIA/TSMC packaging; 4x fewer lasers is a direct hit to laser vendors' unit story.
insights.locator: Spectrum-X Ethernet photonics is the production

themes.theme: Beyond one factory: scale-up, scale-across, XPUs

insights.claim: NVIDIA's scale-up fabric runs on NVLink, where the NVL72 rack forms a 72-GPU scale-up domain that NVIDIA credits with leading tokens per megawatt.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Tokens per megawatt is becoming the buyer metric as power becomes the binding constraint on AI capacity.
insights.locator: NVIDIA’s scale-up networking runs on NVLink

insights.claim: Spectrum-XGS links multiple AI factories with 800Gb/s ports on 102.4Tb/s switches and ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, claiming up to 1.9x lower multi-site latency and doubled scale-across performance for distributed AI.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Multi-site training relaxes the single-campus power constraint, changing where AI datacenters can be sited and how capacity is financed.
insights.locator: Spectrum-XGS reaches across multiple AI factories

insights.claim: NVLink Fusion opens NVIDIA's platform to third-party XPUs, connecting 72 XPUs in one domain at 3.6 TB/s all-to-all bandwidth each, in a cableless MGX rack rated for 45C inlet and 100% liquid cooling with 3x lower latency.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: NVIDIA monetizing rival accelerators through its fabric and rack ecosystem hedges its GPU share risk; custom-ASIC buyers may still pay NVIDIA for interconnect.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's DSX AI-factory software platform (DSX OS, DSX Sim, DSX MaxLPS, DSX Flex) spans power optimization, infrastructure, and platform software, and NVIDIA argues factories need simulation and validation at scale before construction, including cabling planning.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Digital-twin-style pre-construction simulation becomes part of the sale as topologies grow; another software layer deepening platform lock-in.
insights.locator: Software must keep pace with that

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims DSX Air compresses AI-factory deployment timelines from months to days: infrastructure bring-up from six months to one week, infrastructure software from three months to one week, and deployment from two weeks to one day.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Faster time-to-tokens directly improves AI-capex IRR; if real, it accelerates the revenue-recognition cycle for every GPU cluster buildout.
insights.locator: DSX Air compresses that deployment timeline
